segments.text: I want to talk primarily about cases that will come before a

Not

I argue that justice
that does not recognize an offender as a moral agent
is not a good justice system.
The discussion around improvement to the
justice system in recent times
has been about making social variables part of the
assessment in terms of crime and criminality.
What has become more prevalent
has been the increased dependence on the recognition of
particular social, cultural, and political
context. I argue that where these elements enter into
decisions with regard conviction and
sentencings, these disrupt
the principles found in our Western system of justice
in terms of partiality and objectivity.
My observation is based on the writing of Von Hertz, his
censor-based justification for
punishment. For both repentant
or defied offenders, we would not wish to exempt
from blame for either. Both remain moral
agents,
limiting inquiry to questions about his or her choice to
make rational choices.
So I would oppose a view that deemed a group as
being unable to make rational choices.
In the case involving a truck driver in Taranaki killed by a
13-year-old female using his own hammer,
there have been attempts to revisit the crime by lawmakers looking
at variables such as age,
developmental stage, and cognitive function.
Other cases I will mention is the conviction of sexual offenses
by Jayden Meyer, amongst others.
If people are called to desist, there must be a good reason
for supporting
it is wrong.
I'm concerned we are breeding a sense of self-entitlement
among certain offenders. This is, "I can put myself above others,"
and I argue this is setting up a dangerous precedent
in making concessions to popular opinion of
writers such as Leffa.
Treating an actor as someone capable of choice rather than a circus
tiger is a matter of acknowledging his dignity as a human
being.
And while we can have some confidence in the moral judgment that offenders
should be treated as agents capable of choice,
this will not
guarantee that this would lead to a more smooth-running
society, nor even a
society with more social cohesion.
But I reject the notion that it should come at a cost
of the case of justice that I am presenting.

the impression that is left about New Zealand's Criminal Justice
System will be impeded if we have non-legally trained
fact finders sitting essentially as judges as community
magistrates.
The concept that just because the maximum
penalty for something is three months or
under means that it's simple and
straightforward, is a misnomer. Some of the
most complicated issues that affect criminal
justice are charges that are,
on the face of it, not that serious, but do engage real
issues, and our very strong concern is that
community magistrates
have a very strong place in our criminal justice system, yes, but their place
should not be in determining guilt of people
where the maximum penalty is still one that
carries imprisonment.
And whilst, of course, people can have courses and
training, and we recommend and of course support all of that,
the reality is that there would be an inconsistent approach
taken to the judicial background
of different judicial officers in New Zealand.
Family court associates must have seven years as a practicing lawyer.
Associate judges of a high court, obviously legal
experience and substantive legal experience required.
Associate coroners,
practice certificates with at least five years.
And so this reducing the threshold
for community magistrates who have no legal training necessarily
is a deep concern with the perception of justice and the delivery of
justice.
Our concern is that this impedes
on Section 25A of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act in terms of a fair
hearing before an independent and impartial court.
But also New Zealanders are entitled to expect that judicial
officers are legally trained, and
by allowing Clause 22 to pass, you are
essentially saying that that is not so.
And you just have to step back, I think, as well, and think how members of the
